analysis.one_liner: Puts federal health regulation over tobacco: age limits, additive disclosure, tested tar and nicotine levels, tougher warnings.
analysis.headline: The tobacco regulation bill never got a vote: it died in a House subcommittee after sitting for ten months.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new chapter of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act devoted to tobacco. It made it illegal to sell tobacco to anyone under 18, banned free samples and coupon discounts, forced manufacturers to disclose their additives, required the government to test and publish tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels for every brand, and changed the Surgeon General's warning to say plainly that smoking is addictive. It also treated any nicotine product that isn't a tobacco product as a drug. It was introduced in February 1992, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its health subcommittee in March, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, especially young people, gain the most. The bill's own findings note that 60 percent of new smokers are under 14 and that smoking is the single most preventable cause of death in the United States [S3]. It attacks youth smoking at the point of sale (no sales to minors, no free samples or coupons), and it gives consumers honest information — what additives are in their cigarettes and exactly how much tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide each brand delivers [S2]. Non-smokers benefit from reduced overall smoking, and taxpayers benefit from lower health care costs, which the bill says exceed $60 billion a year [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell or give tobacco to anyone under 18 (or a higher state age), and requires states to pass and enforce laws to make that real; if a state fails, the HHS Secretary can step in and regulate how and where tobacco is sold there [S2].
Bans distribution of tobacco as free samples or through coupons and discounts — the industry's main tools for hooking new customers, on which it spent over $2 billion a year [S2].

Requires manufacturers to disclose every additive they put in tobacco products and lets the government ban or reduce unsafe additives, and requires the government to test and publish the tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide, and other harmful constituent levels for every brand before it can be sold [S2].

Changes the Surgeon General's warning to state directly that 'Smoking is Addictive. Once you start you may not be able to stop,' and lets the Secretary strengthen but never weaken warning labels [S3].
Treats nicotine-containing products that are not tobacco as drugs under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, closing a regulatory gap [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers pay the most: compliance costs, disclosure of trade-secret additive formulas, possible bans on additives they currently use, testing requirements for every brand, and the loss of free-sample and coupon marketing. Retailers bear the burden of age verification and enforcement. Some added compliance cost would likely flow into cigarette prices — which for this bill is partly the point, since higher prices discourage smoking.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement scheme leans heavily on the states: the federal ban on youth sales only works if states enact and enforce their own laws, and only after finding state enforcement insufficient can the federal government act — a structure that could delay real results for years [S2].

The bill gives the HHS Secretary very broad discretion — over sales form, manner, and location, additive bans, and labeling — with detailed limits written by regulation rather than statute, which critics of regulatory power would call an over-delegation to unelected officials [S3].

The bill itself acknowledges that lower measured tar, nicotine, or carbon monoxide does not necessarily mean lower health risk, so even full disclosure could mislead smokers into thinking 'lighter' brands are safe [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefits were potentially enormous — the bill targeted the leading preventable cause of death and the pipeline of underage new smokers — and the main costs fell on an industry selling a product its own findings describe as a poisonous addictive drug. The honest weaknesses are design ones: the state-first enforcement structure is slow, and the Secretary's broad discretion invites both overreach and litigation. On balance, the costs to the tobacco industry were the costs the bill intended to impose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 1993 without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Synar introduced the bill on February 27, 1992, with eight original cosponsors including Dick Durbin; 24 members in total signed on, 20 Democrats and 4 Republicans [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced [S5].
On March 23, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — the last action ever recorded; it never reached the full committee or the House floor [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died with it, having never received a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tobacco industry, which continued selling an essentially unregulated product for years: no additive disclosure, no federal brand testing, no federal 'no sale to minors' requirement, and free samples and coupons still legal. Also better off were retailers who avoided age-verification enforcement and anyone whose business depended on tobacco marketing.

for.name: Rep. Mike Synar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled original cosponsors from both parties

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a committee vote

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Fought federal regulation of tobacco through lobbying and litigation throughout this era, spending over $2 billion a year promoting its products

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so the opposition lineup is unknown; support was bipartisan but modest — 24 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 4 Republicans — and the Democratic-led committee that killed it never had to go on record.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected tobacco to food-and-drug-style regulation for the first time: additive disclosure and possible bans, government testing of tar and nicotine for every brand, a ban on free samples and coupons, and a new addiction warning. The industry's business model depended on remaining one of the least regulated consumer products, as the bill's own findings note [S3].

Retailers would face age-verification duties and possible federal rules on the form, manner, and location of sales if state enforcement fell short. Convenience stores and vending operators built revenue on easy access, which is exactly what the bill targeted.

Banning free samples, coupons, and discounting, plus stricter labeling rules, would cut into the $2 billion-plus annual promotion machinery the bill cites. Advertising firms and promotional channels lose that business.

industries.industry: Nicotine replacement and other non-tobacco nicotine products
industries.note: Section 7 deems any nicotine product that is not a tobacco product a drug under the food and drug law, subjecting it to drug approval rules. That raises costs for makers of nicotine gum and similar products but subjects them to safety and efficacy standards consumers rely on.
